cards.front: Recall a key point about Research Methods (Part 1)
cards.back: Experiments test cause-and-effect by manipulating the independent variable (IV) and measuring the dependent variable (DV) while controlling extraneous variables. Types: lab (high control, low ecological validity), field (natural setting, lower control), natural (IV not manipulated), quasi (pre-existing groups).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Research Methods (Part 1)
cards.back: Observations record behaviour without manipulation. Naturalistic: in a natural setting with no intervention. Controlled: some variables regulated. Covert: participants unaware. Overt: participants aware. Participant: researcher joins the group. Non-participant: researcher observes from outside.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Research Methods (Part 1)
cards.back: Correlations measure the relationship between two variables without establishing causation. Positive correlation: both variables increase together. Negative: one increases as the other decreases. Zero: no relationship. Correlation does NOT mean causation.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Research Methods (Part 1)
cards.back: Sampling methods: random (everyone has equal chance), systematic (every nth person), stratified (proportional representation of subgroups), opportunity (whoever is available), volunteer (self-selected). Each has strengths and limitations.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Research Methods (Part 1)
cards.back: Key terms: operationalisation (defining variables precisely so they can be measured), reliability (consistency of results), validity (measuring what was intended), ecological validity (how well findings generalise to real life).

cards.front: What should you know about psychology exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating research methods, consider: control vs realism (lab vs field), generalisability (sampling), ethics (deception, consent), and practical issues (time, cost, access). Always weigh strengths against limitations for the specific research question.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Lab experiments are always the best method because they have the most control over variables. Correct: While lab experiments have high internal validity due to control, they often lack ecological validity - participants behave artificially. cards.front: Key Studies and Theories in Research Methods (Part 1)
cards.back: Research Methods (Part 1) is a core topic in GCSE Psychology that requires understanding of key studies, theories and research methods. The AQA, OCR and Edexcel specifications all require you to know specific studies in detail, evaluate their methodology, and apply psychological concepts to real-life scenarios. cards.front: Applying Research Methods (Part 1) to Real Life
cards.back: GCSE Psychology requires you to apply psychological understanding of research methods (part 1) to everyday situations. Consider how the theories and studies you have learned about explain real behaviour: How does research methods (part 1) affect people in schools, workplaces, families and communities?
